video.title: SpaceX's $2T Case, Nvidia's Shock Selloff, America Turns on AI, Trump Pulls AI Order, Bond Crisis?
video.display_title_html: SpaceX's $2T Case, Nvidia's Shock Selloff, America Turns on AI

thesis: The AI economy is simultaneously generating unprecedented value (Anthropic profitable, SpaceX's $45B Anthropic deal, NVIDIA at $5.3T) while triggering a PR and social crisis driven by dystopian layoff messaging, anti-humanist perception, and possible foreign information campaigns — and the macro backdrop of 310% global debt-to-GDP and rising yields adds a second storm.

insights.headline: Karpathy spent a quarter of his time labeling video data by hand
insights.body: In 2016–17, while leading Full Self-Driving at Tesla, Karpathy spent roughly a quarter of his working hours hand-labeling video frames from Tesla's fleet — embodying what Gavin Baker calls 'commercializing the bitter lesson' before anyone else had. That same first-principles commitment to brute-force data quality is what he now brings to recursive pre-training at Anthropic.

insights.headline: Recursive self-improvement + continual learning = the two final frontiers
insights.body: Gavin Baker identifies the two remaining unsolved problems in AI: (1) recursive self-improvement, where the model influences its own training during a forward pass; and (2) continual learning, where models learn from experience the way humans do. Both remain unsolved; their combination could produce 10× yearly improvement that makes Chamath's projection look conservative. Karpathy's Anthropic role is explicitly focused on (1).

insights.headline: Anthropic + OpenAI combined are on ~$100B ARR at 80% gross margins
insights.body: Per Gavin Baker: the two leading AI labs are at approximately $100B of combined ARR right now with ~80% gross margins on inference, and Anthropic is EBIT-positive. Adding Gemini, Cursor, xAI, and open source, Baker projects $200–300B of ARR across the LLM sector by year-end — validating that the GPU investment cycle has real, immediate ROI, not just circular funding.

insights.headline: Anti-AI sentiment is partly an anti-humanist psychological reaction, not just economics
insights.body: Freeberg argues a third driver of AI backlash, beyond economics and foreign influence: AI is fundamentally non-human-centric in a way that 'shifts and f***s with the ego.' The Copernican parallel — heliocentricity dethroned Earth, AI dethrones human cognitive supremacy — creates a deep psychological rejection. It doesn't cause the backlash but amplifies it in ways that can't be addressed with economic reassurances alone.

insights.headline: Zuckerberg recorded employees to train AI, then laid them off — and said it publicly
insights.body: Meta placed recording software on all employees' computers to capture workflows and train AI models, simultaneously laying off ~8,000 people. In his own words, Zuckerberg explained that internal engineers produce better training data than contractors. Workers who had built AI tools to improve their own productivity were then included in layoffs — creating the perception that efficiency gains accelerated their own replacements.

insights.headline: Anthropic is paying SpaceX $1.25B/month — $45B over three years
insights.body: SpaceX's S-1 reveals Anthropic has signed a $45B deal (15B/year, $1.25B/month) to rent Colossus 1 and parts of Colossus 2. This effectively means SpaceX has already added a second Starlink-scale revenue stream from a single customer. The deal has a 90-day cancellation clause by either party, meaning Elon could reclaim the compute or Anthropic could find alternatives.

insights.headline: SpaceX builds data centers 46% faster each iteration: 122, 91, 66 days
insights.body: SpaceX's S-1 discloses accelerating data center construction times: Colossus 1 took 122 days, Colossus 2 took 91 days, Colossus 3 took 66 days. The trend line is a learning curve, not a one-off. Gavin Baker's implication: with Anthropic as a clear off-take partner, SpaceX can now 'stamp out' data centers at a pace no hyperscaler can match, giving it a structural cost and speed advantage in the emerging cloud-for-AI market.

insights.headline: Cursor has more coding tokens than exist on the public internet
insights.body: Per Gavin Baker, a stat from over a year ago: Cursor allegedly holds more tokens of coding data than exist anywhere on the public internet. Three to four weeks of reinforcement learning on Colossus 2 using that data pushed Cursor's Composer 2.5 to Pareto-dominant status on coding benchmarks — establishing it as the most-selected model on the Cursor platform before a new base model has even been trained with it.

insights.headline: The AI market is cross-sectionally inefficient: chips and cooling can't both be right
insights.body: Gavin Baker's key investing insight: memory companies trade at 3–5× PE, NVIDIA trades at low-teens PE, and power/cooling/optical infrastructure trades at much higher multiples. These valuations imply contradictory scenarios — if infrastructure multiples are correct, NVIDIA and memory are dramatically undervalued; if NVIDIA's multiple is correct, infrastructure is overvalued. The market can't be right on both sides simultaneously.

insights.headline: NVIDIA projected a $20B CPU business this year — overnight became a top-3 CPU maker
insights.body: Buried in NVIDIA's Q1 earnings: the company projected $20 billion in CPU revenue for fiscal year 2026. That would make NVIDIA one of the world's largest CPU manufacturers within a single year of entering the market at scale. The mechanism is co-design with every major AI lab — NVIDIA is the only company that sits inside all of their training and inference architectures simultaneously.

insights.headline: Older GPUs could have 10–15 year useful lives when paired with newer ASICs for decode
insights.body: The bear thesis that GPU amortization schedules are too aggressive (Burry argued 2-year true lifespan) may be inverted. As domain-specific accelerators like Groq or Cerebras handle the decode stage of inference, older GPUs become useful compute for the prefill stage. CoreWeave is signing 6-year contracts at 6% financing rates — customers wouldn't do that if they believed 2-year lifespan. The real lifespan may be 10–15 years in a mixed architecture.

insights.headline: The harness is as important as the model in the agentic era
insights.body: Grok lacked a harness — a runtime that manages state, memory, and integrations — while Claude had Claude Code and OpenAI had Codex. The release of Grok Build is therefore as significant as a model release. Baker and Chamath argue the harness and model must now be co-developed: a frontier model without a harness is 'like using a basic chatbot from a year ago.' This reframes competitive analysis: benchmark position alone is insufficient.

insights.headline: Orbital compute becomes commercially real in second half of 2028 to early 2030
insights.body: Gavin Baker's point prediction for orbital compute: second half 2028 to first half 2030. There is already a working H100 in space today (Karpathy trained a model and ran inference on it). NVIDIA is building a space-designed GPU variant. SpaceX's key underappreciated advantage: they use non-radiation-hardened commercial semiconductors that happen to pass rad testing, keeping cost dramatically lower than traditional space hardware.

insights.headline: Strait of Hormuz closure is relatively good for America — oil shock as forced reindustrialization
insights.body: Gavin Baker frames the Iran-driven Strait closure as asymmetrically bad for Europe, Japan, and China (which need Middle Eastern oil) and relatively good for the US, which is now the world's largest oil and gas exporter. Every day the Strait is closed is a forcing function for US reindustrialization, makes American electricity cheaper than global peers (natural gas is down while LNG is up 100–200%), and aligns with Trump's policy goals — which is why Baker argues Trump is in no hurry to resolve it.
